Return Of Part II: Strategy

Chapter 4 Preliminary draft

The Strategy Menu

Thirteen named strategies, rated by risk and effort.

A strategy you have not named is a strategy you cannot follow, measure, or drop. This chapter lists thirteen named strategies and rates each one by risk and effort, so every trade you place belongs to something you chose on purpose.

Why name strategies at all

Most losing habits hide inside vague language. “I was just trading” covers a patient value purchase, a chart breakout, and a same-day gamble. They have different risks, different time frames, and different ways to be wrong. Lump them together and the journal cannot tell you which one is working.

A name fixes that. Once a trade is tagged “Swing Trading” or “Covered Calls”, you can ask real questions. Did I follow the rules for this strategy? What was the result across all trades of this type? Should this strategy get more of my attention, or none? The journal in Chapter 12 depends on these tags.

The menu

The table lists all thirteen strategies in a fixed order. The numbers are labels, not ranks. They stay the same through the rest of the book.

How to read risk and effort

Risk asks how much you can lose, and how fast, when you are wrong. A broad index fund can fall a long way, but it holds many companies at once, so no single failure sinks it. An option that expires the same day can lose nearly all its value within minutes. Risk here describes the shape of the loss, not a forecast.

Effort asks how much attention the strategy demands. Some strategies are cheap to run once they are set up. Value and Systematic cost a lot of work at the start and little afterward. Day Trading and 0DTE Scalping cost a lot of work every single day.

Read the two columns together. Low risk and low effort suits money you cannot afford to lose. High risk and very high effort suits only a small slice that you have already decided you can lose. Two entries break the pattern. Protective Hedge is rated “Lowers risk” because it exists to insure other positions. Systematic is rated “Depends on rules” because software only repeats what you tell it, good or bad.

How the strategies group

  • Passive core (1 to 3): Index Core, Custom Pie, Dividend Growth. Low effort, low to moderate risk. This is the base of the portfolio.
  • Patient active (4): Value. You do the work up front, then wait.
  • Active satellite (5 and 9): Growth Momentum and Swing Trading. Short-to-medium holding periods, with stops and a written plan for every entry.
  • Options from the seller's side (6 and 7): Covered Calls and the Wheel. You collect payments and let time work for you.
  • Insurance (8): Protective Hedge. It costs money in calm markets and pays in bad ones.
  • The casino floor (10 to 12): Long Options, Day Trading, 0DTE Scalping. High risk, high effort, funded only by a fixed tuition budget.
  • Systematic (13): Rules written once and run by software. It sits beside the others rather than above them.

The menu is a menu, not a to-do list.

A menu, not a to-do list

You are not meant to run all thirteen. Each strategy needs its own rules, its own journal tag, and its own share of your attention. Spread across too many, you will do none of them well.

Later chapters cover each group: the core in Chapter 6, the satellite in Chapter 7, options from the seller's side in Chapter 8, the casino floor in Chapter 9, and Systematic in Chapter 15. Chapter 5 sets the order in which you may add them, and what you must prove before moving on.

Open questions

  • Which of the thirteen strategies fit your edge from Chapter 3, and which only look attractive?
  • Do the risk and effort ratings still hold once you have real journal data on each strategy?
  • How many strategies can you run at once before the quality of your attention drops?
  • Should the Protective Hedge be tied to a fixed trigger, such as the size of the core, or left to judgment?
